Arcade setup

Choose which conditions can come up in Arcade mode, and how many rounds a run should use. Each Regular/Irregular slot's dropdown picks which of its 12 transpositions plays; with more than one run configured, "Customize per run" lets you assign a different transposition to each run instead of repeating the same one.

Picking a template fills in that batch's exact conditions/runs/miss-timeout/gap settings below, so you can generate another export for the same batch without re-entering everything. Templates live in inFiles/batchTemplates.json when a data folder is connected (above), or load a templates file manually here.

The IRB dropdown lists any file with “IRB” in its name found in inFiles/ (connect a data folder above to populate it). Whichever one is selected here is baked into the exported file below and shown to the subject as a consent screen — with Continue / Decline buttons — before they can enter their name and info. Leave it on “no IRB form” to export without a consent gate, exactly as before.

Number of runs
Miss timeout
A target left untouched this long auto-advances and counts as a miss.
Jam duration
Seconds — the practice jam session after each round (not the grand finale).
Finale duration
Seconds — the grand finale at the end of each run.
Gap after response
Ms — fixed pause between a response (target disappears) and the next target appearing.
Start randoms
How many random targets open a condition, before the learned sequence begins.
End randoms
How many random targets close a condition, after the learned sequence ends.
Sequence reps
How many times the learned sequence (e.g. 8 targets) repeats between the start and end randoms.
Add jitter to that gap?
Include a practice round?
Include visitor practice?
After the allotted runs finish?

Finite: once the configured number of runs is done, the participant sees a true end-of-study exit screen and cannot start another run. Infinity: that screen is replaced by one welcoming them to reshuffle and play again, with a clearly separate "Exit study" button whenever they're ready to stop — useful when you'd like to encourage as much additional data as participants are willing to give.

Practice miss timeout
Same idea as the real miss timeout above, but its own separate value used only during the practice round.
Practice gap after response
Ms — same idea as the real response gap above, but its own separate value used only during the practice round.
Number of Random Targets
How many correct presses in a row, with zero wrong keys, the participant must string together to pass the practice round. Up to 4× this many total presses are allowed before a practice attempt is called off and the instructions are shown again.

Which pair of validated sets (plus that collection's Monotonic/Silent controls) the grid below shows, Arcade runs use, and the Lab-mode Stimuli panel plays. 1-Cadence Sets resolve once (position 5); 2-Cadence Sets chunk into two groups, each ending on the tonic (press 4 & 8). Switching rebuilds this grid and the Lab-mode picker to match.

Generates a locked copy of this page: fullscreen on start, only the conditions/runs/batch/miss-timeout configured above, no way back to Lab mode, and the current leaderboard standings baked in so they can see where they'd rank. If a data folder is connected (above), it saves straight into outFiles/ next to the root HTML file; otherwise it downloads normally. Send it to someone — they open it, play, and click “Save my results (.json)” after their run to send back their full round-by-round data. Drop that returned file into inFiles/completedSubData/ (or load it manually above) to fold it into your leaderboard and make it available in the Subject Data & Plots panel.

Subject data & plots

Populated automatically from the connected folder, or from files loaded via “Load leaderboard” below.

Conditions:

The strip along the bottom marks trial phase: gray for learned-sequence trials, black for random ones. The bar chart on the right shows the "end difference" for the same selection — the last random-block RT minus the last learned-block RT, so higher/above zero means learned trials were faster at the end. One bar per condition, split further by run if “All runs” is selected.

Same box-plot style as above, but counting what happened during the learned-sequence trials specifically, per round: misses (left, a target left untouched until it timed out) and wrong-key presses (right, any incorrect key hit before the correct one). One box per condition, split further by run if “All runs” is selected.

Same selection as the plots above (batch/subject/condition/run), one box per run: real measured time each round's participant spent with the window unfocused, with each matching round shown as its own jittered dot. Computed from the session's own blur/focus timestamps (focusEventLog), clipped to each round's actual start/end window — not an estimate from trial counts. Only available for files that include a focusEventLog field at all; older loaded files won't contribute any dots here.

RT by sequence position (1–8), learned-sequence (phase L) trials only, using only each round's last min(4, reps) repetitions and excluding misses/away-flagged trials. Left: 1-Cadence Sets (Legacy A/B, Progression-Generalization C/D, plus their Monotonic/Silent controls) — single authentic cadence highlighted at position 5. Right: 2-Cadence Sets (wx W/X, uv U/V, plus their own Monotonic2C/silent2C controls) — two group cadences highlighted at positions 4 and 8. Each box is the distribution of per-subject mean RT at that position/run/condition combination — exactly one dot per subject (a subject contributing more than one matching round to the same combination has those rounds' means averaged together first, rather than plotting one dot per round) — split further by run if “All runs” is selected. Requires a seqIdx field on trials; files/rounds/trials that predate it are silently skipped rather than plotted as zero.

Diagnostic overview, not tied to the condition/subject/run filters above: one horizontal box plot per batch currently loaded, showing how many total runs each subject in that batch has completed (x-axis), with every subject plotted as its own jittered dot. Useful for spotting batches with unusually high dropout (most dots clustered near a low run count) or unusually high engagement (dots spread out toward high run counts, likely from infinity mode).

Match length: 3 4 5 6 7 8+

Spontaneous sequence replay during practice jams (never the grand finale): a run of 3+ consecutive H/J/K/L presses, gap-broken at 1s of idle time between presses, that also appears as a contiguous (cyclically-wrapped) stretch of a learned condition sequence trained so far this attempt. Pooled across every subject currently loaded (respects only the batch filter above, not subject/condition/run) — one bar per condition actually run by anyone in the pool, plus a final "Ambiguous / multiple" bar for any match consistent with more than one condition (never double-counted into both). Each bar's segments show the distribution of matched lengths within it, not just a raw total. Only available for files that include a sequenceReplayLog field at all; older loaded files won't contribute here.

Today's Study

You will perform two tasks today. You'll practice each separately before either one counts. There are no surprises.

Task one is your day job: a shift at the button-pressing factory, punching in and pressing keys for a paycheck. Task two is your music career: practicing your tunes, winning fans over, and rocking their sox off at your shows.

Every dollar you earn at the factory becomes something real on tour. Work the day job well, and the tour gets bigger and better.

Think you can make it to the top?

Here's the board as it stands. Give it your best shot and see where you land!

Button Factory Training

That attempt did not meet the required criteria. Please try again.

Before your first shift at the factory you will complete a short practice trial to confirm you understand the task. A red target will appear in one of four locations. Each location corresponds to a key on the keyboard, arranged left to right: . Your objective is to respond as quickly as possible without making an error.

To proceed, you must respond correctly to 10 consecutive targets, each within the time limit. An incorrect response or a missed target will reset the count to zero.

During the task pressing a key will sometimes produce a sound and sometimes will not. This is expected and does not indicate an error.

How to Win Over Fans

Your second task is your music career. Practice jams that build up to real, live shows in front of a crowd.

Visitors will wander into your practice jams uninvited, but if you play the way they like, they'll remember you and turn up to your shows. Watch the speech bubble above each one while you play. Green means you've won them over, yellow means you're getting warmer, and red means not yet.

This is a practice session. Three visitors will appear, one at a time, so you can learn what each one wants before any of it counts.

Each one is looking for something different: a steady beat, a specific rhythm, or a moment of quiet. Watch the speech bubble to see what it's asking for. A metronome click will help you keep time.

1 of 3: Steve

Keep a steady beat on H, J, K, or L.

👀 Keep an eye out!

During your jam sessions, some special visitors might wander in to check out your moves. Play the way they like it while they're watching to impress them — do that, and they'll show up at your big finale, ready to party! Don't sweat it if you can't win them all over, though — there are lots of them, each wants something different, and you likely won't be able to satisfy every visitor. You'll learn who's who as you win them over.

Disappointing the Landlord or the Old Folks badly enough can bring the Police down on your very next gig. Once they show up, nobody else does — no other visitor will come around while they're there.

A few things worth knowing: this page needs to stay open in your browser to keep going — if you close the window (or your computer restarts, loses power, etc.), there's no way to pick back up where you left off, and starting again means opening this file fresh from the beginning. You do not need an internet connection at any point to play — everything runs locally in your browser once the page is open. And if you've opened and closed this file more than once during this study (rather than keeping one window open the whole time), you'll end up with more than one results file saved on your computer — please send back all of them, not just the most recent one.
